ground_truth.mechanism: The new suite never checks that the temp file name is unique per write. If someone later changes it to a fixed name, the suite still passes, yet a temp file left behind by a crash would make every later O_EXCL create raise FileExistsError, and spotify_auth.access_token swallows that OSError, so a rotated refresh token would be silently lost.
ground_truth.evidence: pooled cluster p4: 2 reviewer finding(s), ruled valid once by the blinded Opus ruling with the code (its evidence is in the pool file)
ground_truth.source: pooled cluster p4, accepted by lead on 2026-10-23

non_issues.claim: Each crash between creating the randomly named temp file and the rename leaves another secret-bearing temp file behind, and nothing ever cleans these up.
non_issues.why_not: The spec for this change (SEC-4) says to move the existing `browser/host._write_private` recipe into a shared module: a uniquely named temporary file opened with O_EXCL|O_NOFOLLOW at 0600, fsynced, swapped in with os.replace, and unlinked on any failure it can catch. The module docstring also says a crash leftover is never reused. That recipe was already in host.py, stt_settings and subagents before this change, so the random temporary name is the intended design. A SIGKILL between create and rename is the one failure no in-process cleanup can catch, and the file it leaves stays 0600 in an owner-only folder, so nothing becomes readable to anyone else. Leftovers can only pile up through repeated kills in that brief window, which is a cleanup nicety rather than a defect the change introduces.
non_issues.source: pooled cluster p1, ruled invalid, accepted as a non-issue by lead on 2026-10-23

non_issues.claim: The sub-agent record writer opens its file for append without O_NOFOLLOW, so a symlink planted at the record path makes it write into the file the link points to, and no test covers this path.
non_issues.why_not: The append at subagents.py:637 is old code that this change did not touch. The SEC-4 spec deliberately limits the sub-agent fix to `_compact` (missing O_NOFOLLOW/fsync), and that function now calls write_private. The sub-agent record is not a credential file. Planting a symlink requires write access to the owner's private thread folder, and an attacker with that access already controls the state. So the change neither introduced nor was asked to fix a defect here.
non_issues.source: pooled cluster p2, ruled invalid, accepted as a non-issue by lead on 2026-10-23

non_issues.claim: The Onshape credential bundle is created with the default umask mode and only narrowed to 0600 afterwards, and it follows symlinks; this is the same flaw the change fixed for the other writers.
non_issues.why_not: The diff never touches jarvis/onshape_auth.py, so this is old code and not something the change introduced or made worse. The SEC-4 spec for this change limits its scope to the Discord, Google, Spotify, sub-agent and STT writers and does not list onshape_auth.py. The exposure the findings describe also doesn't hold up. Line 230 sets the parent folder ~/.config/jarvis to 0700 before write_text runs, so no other user can open the file while it is still at the umask mode, and only the owner can plant a symlink in that folder. The spec itself calls this the 'real exposure is small' case for google_auth. The reviewers are suggesting a follow-up outside this change's scope, not pointing to a defect in it.
non_issues.source: pooled cluster p3, ruled invalid, accepted as a non-issue by lead on 2026-10-23

non_issues.claim: The open-flags check does not require O_CLOEXEC, so removing it and leaking the token file descriptor to child processes would go undetected.
non_issues.why_not: The test gap could not cause the leak the finding describes. Since PEP 446 (Python 3.4), os.open makes every new descriptor non-inheritable, which sets close-on-exec at the OS level whether or not O_CLOEXEC is passed. So removing the flag would not let the token descriptor reach exec'd children, and the project runs Python 3.14. A forked child inherits descriptors either way, because close-on-exec only acts at exec. The descriptor is also closed before write_private returns. An extra assertion on O_CLOEXEC would guard a redundant flag, so the missing assertion is not a defect.
non_issues.source: pooled cluster p5, ruled invalid, accepted as a non-issue by lead on 2026-10-23

non_issues.claim: The Spotify rotation test only checks the final file contents and mode, so it does not catch a change that saves the rotated token after the access token has already been returned.
non_issues.why_not: The reviewer's mutation moves `_store(bundle)` below `_cached_token = payload["access_token"]`, but the token still only reaches the caller at the `return` on line 174. Both orders run inside the same `_lock` block before that return, so a crash at any point stops the token from being handed back either way. The two orders behave the same, and no test can or needs to tell them apart. A change that really saved the token after `access_token()` returned, or skipped saving it, would leave the old refresh token on disk when the test reads the file after the call (lines 534-540), so the check would catch it. The test checks the property the rule is about, and the gap described is not a real defect.
non_issues.source: pooled cluster p6, ruled invalid, accepted as a non-issue by lead on 2026-10-23

non_issues.claim: The Google writer tests need to bind a loopback HTTP server, so where networking is restricted they fail before they reach the file-writing code they are meant to test.
non_issues.why_not: The test drives the real google_auth.connect loopback OAuth callback on an ephemeral 127.0.0.1 port, using a fake browser and a fake httpx.post. That is what the project's test rules prescribe: temporary config, fake providers and ephemeral ports, never the live ports. A sandbox that forbids binding loopback sockets is a limit of the reviewer's environment, not a defect in the change. If the test did fail there, it would fail loudly as a counted failure and would not pass falsely.
